Text: The rapid exam — a head-to-toe sweep to identify life threats — is performed right after the {{c2::primary assessment::assessment phase}} and should take no more than {{c1::90}} seconds.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the rapid exam is not a focused assessment — it is a fast sweep for any additional injuries.

Why: injuries the sweep identifies must be managed prior to transport.

Text:
In the rapid exam you look and feel for DCAP-BTLS at every body region:

{{c1::Deformity::D}}

{{c1::Contusions::C}}

{{c1::Abrasions::A}}

{{c1::Punctures::P}}

{{c1::Burns::B}}

{{c1::Tenderness::T}}

{{c1::Lacerations::L}}

{{c1::Swelling::S}}
Back Extra:
Mnemonic: DCAP-BTLS — inspect and palpate for all eight findings at every stop of the head-to-toe sweep.

Why: the sweep exists to catch additional injuries that must be managed prior to transport.

Text:
Rapid exam, the head and the abdomen — the extra checks beyond DCAP-BTLS:

Head → also assess the {{c1::pupils}}

Abdomen → palpate for {{c1::rigidity (firm or soft)}} and {{c1::distention}}
Back Extra:
Why: a distended or firm abdomen can identify an internal hemorrhage — an indication for immediate transport.

Roster: rapid exam extras — head (pupils) → neck (JVD, tracheal deviation, spinal step-off) → chest (wall movement, crepitus, subcutaneous emphysema, equal rise/fall + breath sounds) → abdomen (rigidity, distention) → pelvis (compress only if no pain) → extremities (distal pulses, motor, sensory) → back/buttocks (in-line roll, check before loading)

Text:
Rapid exam, the neck — beyond DCAP-BTLS, look and feel for:

{{c1::jugular venous distention (JVD)}}

{{c1::tracheal deviation from midline}}

{{c1::spinal step-off (a vertebra out of line with the rest)}}
Back Extra:
Cue: the neck's three extras follow its midline anatomy — vein, airway, spine.

Roster: rapid exam extras — head (pupils) → neck (JVD, tracheal deviation, spinal step-off) → chest (wall movement, crepitus, subcutaneous emphysema, equal rise/fall + breath sounds) → abdomen (rigidity, distention) → pelvis (compress only if no pain) → extremities (distal pulses, motor, sensory) → back/buttocks (in-line roll, check before loading)

Text:
Rapid exam, the chest — beyond DCAP-BTLS there are four look/feel checks:

{{c1::chest wall movement}}

{{c1::crepitus}}

{{c1::subcutaneous emphysema}}

{{c1::equal rise and fall}}

…then {{c2::listen to breath sounds}} on both sides.
Back Extra:
Cue: eyes and hands do the four; the ears finish the chest.

Roster: rapid exam extras — head (pupils) → neck (JVD, tracheal deviation, spinal step-off) → chest (wall movement, crepitus, subcutaneous emphysema, equal rise/fall + breath sounds) → abdomen (rigidity, distention) → pelvis (compress only if no pain) → extremities (distal pulses, motor, sensory) → back/buttocks (in-line roll, check before loading)

Text: Rapid exam, the pelvis — look for DCAP-BTLS; compress the pelvis only if the patient has {{c1::no pain::pain / no pain}}: palms over the {{c2::iliac crests::bony landmark}}, pressing gently {{c2::downward and inward::two directions}}, checking for tenderness and instability.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: pain at the pelvis means skip the compression — the squeeze is a test reserved for the pain-free pelvis.

Roster: rapid exam extras — head (pupils) → neck (JVD, tracheal deviation, spinal step-off) → chest (wall movement, crepitus, subcutaneous emphysema, equal rise/fall + breath sounds) → abdomen (rigidity, distention) → pelvis (compress only if no pain) → extremities (distal pulses, motor, sensory) → back/buttocks (in-line roll, check before loading)

Text: A fall victim's rapid exam reaches the pelvis, and he winces with pain as you palpate it. Do you compress the iliac crests to test stability? {{c1::No::yes / no}}
Back Extra: Why: the compression test is gated on a pain-free pelvis — palpation pain is already a positive finding (the T in DCAP-BTLS).

Text:
Rapid exam, all four extremities — beyond DCAP-BTLS, assess bilaterally for:

{{c1::distal pulses}}

{{c1::motor function}}

{{c1::sensory function}}
Back Extra:
Cue: circulation, movement, feeling — each checked side against side.

Roster: rapid exam extras — head (pupils) → neck (JVD, tracheal deviation, spinal step-off) → chest (wall movement, crepitus, subcutaneous emphysema, equal rise/fall + breath sounds) → abdomen (rigidity, distention) → pelvis (compress only if no pain) → extremities (distal pulses, motor, sensory) → back/buttocks (in-line roll, check before loading)

Text: Rapid exam, the back and buttocks — in all trauma patients, roll the patient onto the side while maintaining {{c1::in-line stabilization of the spine::spine precaution}}, rolling in {{c1::one motion}}; check the back before you {{c2::load the patient for transport}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: the one-motion roll is the log roll — spine held in line, a single smooth turn.

Roster: rapid exam extras — head (pupils) → neck (JVD, tracheal deviation, spinal step-off) → chest (wall movement, crepitus, subcutaneous emphysema, equal rise/fall + breath sounds) → abdomen (rigidity, distention) → pelvis (compress only if no pain) → extremities (distal pulses, motor, sensory) → back/buttocks (in-line roll, check before loading)

Text:
Eight conditions make a patient high priority — transport immediately. The four that flag failing consciousness or ABCs:

{{c1::Unresponsive}}

{{c1::Altered LOC (level of consciousness)}}

{{c1::Difficulty breathing}}

{{c1::Uncontrolled bleeding}}
Back Extra:
Why: priority designation decides whether the patient gets immediate transport or can tolerate a few more minutes on scene.

Roster: high-priority conditions — unresponsive; difficulty breathing; uncontrolled bleeding; altered LOC; severe chest pain; pale skin or other signs of poor perfusion; complicated childbirth; severe pain in any area of the body

Text:
Eight conditions make a patient high priority — transport immediately. The other four, beyond consciousness and the ABCs:

{{c1::Severe chest pain}}

{{c1::Pale skin or other signs of poor perfusion}}

{{c1::Complicated childbirth}}

{{c1::Severe pain in any area of the body}}
Back Extra:
Cue: two are severe pain (chest, or anywhere), one is the skin announcing poor perfusion, one is a birth in trouble.

Roster: high-priority conditions — unresponsive; difficulty breathing; uncontrolled bleeding; altered LOC; severe chest pain; pale skin or other signs of poor perfusion; complicated childbirth; severe pain in any area of the body

Text: A 45-year-old reports severe chest pain; his ABCs are intact and he is fully alert. Transport priority? {{c1::High — transport immediately::high / medium / low}}
Back Extra: Why: severe chest pain is on the high-priority list even with intact ABCs — priority designation asks whether he can tolerate a few more minutes on scene, and a high-priority patient cannot.

Text: {{c1::The Golden Hour}}, also called the {{c1::Golden Period}}, is the time from {{c2::injury}} to {{c2::definitive care}}, during which treatment of shock and traumatic injuries must occur to maximize the chance of survival.
Back Extra: Why: over time the body has increasing difficulty compensating for shock and traumatic injuries — so spend as little time as possible on scene in significant or severe trauma.

Text: En route, reassess vital signs every {{c1::15}} minutes if the patient is stable, and every {{c1::5}} minutes (or as often as the situation permits) if unstable — until you reach the ED.
Back Extra:
Why: serial vitals reveal trends in the patient's condition — a single reading cannot.

Pitfall: do not be falsely reassured by apparently normal vital signs — the body compensates powerfully for severe injury or illness.

Text: Your patient's condition is worsening during transport, vitals trending down. How often do you reassess vital signs? {{c1::Every 5 minutes::interval}} — or as often as the situation permits.
Back Extra: Cue: unstable = every 5 min; stable = every 15 min — the unstable patient earns the tighter loop.

Text: Treating a patient for shock before {{c1::the blood pressure drops::vital-sign event}} increases the chance of survival.
Back Extra:
Why: even severe trauma can show fairly normal vitals at first; when compensation fails — decompensated shock — vitals deteriorate rapidly, especially in children.

Cue: the rapid fall at decompensation is exactly why vitals are rechecked so often.

Text: A motorcyclist has obvious severe trauma, but his vital signs are still fairly normal. When should you begin treating him for shock? {{c1::Immediately — before the blood pressure drops::right away / once BP falls}}
Back Extra: Why: normal early vitals can be compensation, not stability — treating before the pressure drops is what buys survival.

Text: Two responders arrive at a scene with bystanders. To gather history without delaying care, one {{c1::questions the people in the vicinity}} while the other {{c1::initiates the patient assessment}}.
Back Extra:
Why: history from family, friends, and bystanders may be unobtainable once transport begins — collect it on scene.

Cue: also check for medical identification tags and paperwork about the events leading up.
